title: Special Purpose (Subsidiary) Books
description: Class 11 Accountancy: special purpose subsidiary books — purchases, sales, purchases return and sales return books, bills receivable/payable books, journal proper, and trade vs cash discount with GST.

topics.title: Subsidiary Books: Purchases, Sales and Returns Books
topics.concept:
As a business grows, recording every credit purchase and sale in the journal becomes impractical. So similar transactions are grouped into special purpose books (also called subsidiary books or books of original entry). Each book records one type of transaction. The benefits are division of labour, less bulky records, and easier reference.

The main subsidiary books for goods are:

  • Purchases Book — records credit purchases of goods only (goods meant for resale). It does not record cash purchases (those go in the cash book) or the purchase of assets (those go in the journal proper).
  • Sales Book — records credit sales of goods only. Cash sales go in the cash book; the sale of an asset goes in the journal proper.
  • Purchases Return (Return Outward) Book — records goods returned to suppliers. A debit note is the source document.
  • Sales Return (Return Inward) Book — records goods returned by customers. A credit note is the source document.

Each book is totalled periodically and the total is posted to the relevant account: the Purchases Book total → debit of Purchases A/c; the Sales Book total → credit of Sales A/c; and the individual parties are posted to their personal accounts. The classic trap to remember: only credit transactions in goods go to these books — cash deals go to the cash book, and assets/other items go to the journal proper.

examples.problem: Example 1: In which book is a credit purchase of goods recorded?
examples.solution:
Credit, goods.

  • Credit purchase of goods → Purchases Book.

examples.problem: Example 2: A cash sale of goods is made. Is it recorded in the Sales Book?
examples.solution:
No — cash goes elsewhere.

  • The Sales Book records only credit sales.
  • A cash sale is recorded in the cash book.
examples.answer: No — cash sales go in the cash book; the Sales Book is for credit sales only.

examples.problem: Example 3: Goods are returned to a supplier. Which book and which source document?
examples.solution:
Return outward.

  • Goods returned to a supplier → Purchases Return Book.
  • Source document: debit note.
examples.answer: The Purchases Return (Return Outward) Book; the source document is a debit note.

recap:
• Subsidiary books group similar transactions: Purchases Book (credit purchases of goods), Sales Book (credit sales), Purchases Return (to suppliers, debit note), Sales Return (from customers, credit note).
  • Trap: only credit transactions in goods; cash → cash book; assets/others → journal proper.

quiz.q: Credit sales of goods are recorded in the:
quiz.explanation: The sales book records credit sales of goods only.

quiz.q: Goods returned by a customer are recorded in the:
quiz.explanation: Customer returns go in the sales return (return inward) book.

topics.title: Bills Receivable, Bills Payable Books and the Journal Proper
topics.concept:
Two more subsidiary books deal with bills of exchange (studied fully in a later chapter):

  • Bills Receivable Book — records the bills of exchange received by the firm (bills we will collect money on). The total is posted to the debit of the Bills Receivable A/c.
  • Bills Payable Book — records the bills accepted/issued by the firm (bills we must pay). The total is posted to the credit of the Bills Payable A/c.

That makes eight common subsidiary books in all: cash book, purchases book, sales book, purchases return book, sales return book, bills receivable book, bills payable book — and finally the journal proper.

The journal proper (or general journal) is the catch-all: it records every transaction that does not fit into any of the special books. This includes:

  • Opening entries and closing entries;
  • Adjusting entries (outstanding, prepaid, depreciation);
  • Rectifying entries for errors;
  • Transfer entries;
  • Credit purchase or sale of assets (e.g. buying machinery on credit) — not goods, so not the purchases/sales book;
  • Other non-routine items like goods taken by the owner for personal use.

So the system works like a sorting office: routine cash, credit-goods and bills transactions each go to their own book, and everything unusual goes to the journal proper. Knowing which book a transaction belongs to is one of the most-tested skills in this chapter.

examples.problem: Example 1: A firm buys machinery on credit. In which book is it recorded?
examples.solution:
Asset on credit, not goods.

  • It is not goods, so not the purchases book.
  • A credit purchase of an asset goes in the journal proper.
examples.answer: The journal proper (it is an asset bought on credit, not goods).

examples.problem: Example 2: Where are bills of exchange received recorded?
examples.solution:
Bills we will collect.

  • Bills received → Bills Receivable Book.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name two types of entry recorded in the journal proper.
examples.solution:
Non-routine entries.

  • Opening/closing entries, adjusting entries, rectifying entries, transfer entries.
examples.answer: Any two of: opening, closing, adjusting, rectifying or transfer entries (also credit purchase/sale of assets).

recap:
• Bills Receivable Book (bills received → B/R A/c Dr); Bills Payable Book (bills accepted → B/P A/c Cr).
  • Journal proper = catch-all: opening, closing, adjusting, rectifying, transfer entries and credit purchase/sale of assets.
  • Eight subsidiary books in total; the skill is choosing the right book.

quiz.q: A credit purchase of furniture (an asset) is recorded in the:
quiz.explanation: Assets bought on credit go in the journal proper, not the purchases book.

quiz.q: Bills accepted by the firm are recorded in the:
quiz.explanation: Bills the firm must pay go in the bills payable book.

topics.title: Trade Discount, Cash Discount and GST in Subsidiary Books
topics.concept:
Two kinds of discount appear in trade, and students must keep them apart.

 Trade discountCash discount
Why givenon the list price, for buying in bulkto encourage prompt/early payment
Recorded in books?No — only the net amount is recordedYes — recorded as discount allowed/received
Shown onthe invoice (deducted)at the time of payment

So in the purchases/sales books we record the amount after deducting trade discount; trade discount itself never appears as a separate account. Cash discount, by contrast, is recorded (in the cash book) only when payment is actually made.

Modern subsidiary books also handle GST (Goods and Services Tax). On an intra-state sale, the seller charges CGST + SGST; on an inter-state sale, IGST. In the sales/purchases books, the GST is shown in separate columns:

  • On a sale, the firm collects output GST — a liability owed to the government.
  • On a purchase, the firm pays input GST — which it can set off (input tax credit) against output GST.

For example, goods sold for Rs 10,000 with 18% GST inside a state means CGST Rs 900 + SGST Rs 900, so the customer is billed Rs 11,800; the firm owes Rs 1,800 GST to the government (after setting off any input credit). Adding GST columns keeps the subsidiary books accurate and tax-compliant — exactly how real businesses record sales today.

examples.problem: Example 1: List price Rs 20,000, trade discount 10%. At what amount is the purchase recorded?
examples.solution:
Record net of trade discount.

  • Trade discount = 10% of 20,000 = 2,000.
  • Recorded amount = 20,000 − 2,000 = Rs 18,000.
examples.answer: Rs 18,000 (list price less 10% trade discount); trade discount itself is not recorded separately.

examples.problem: Example 2: Which discount is recorded in the books — trade or cash?
examples.solution:
Cash discount.

  • Trade discount is not recorded (only the net amount is).
  • Cash discount is recorded (discount allowed/received).
examples.answer: Cash discount is recorded; trade discount is not.

examples.problem: Example 3: Goods sold within the state for Rs 5,000 at 18% GST. Find the CGST and SGST.
examples.answer: CGST Rs 450 and SGST Rs 450 (total GST Rs 900); the customer is billed Rs 5,900.

recap:
• Trade discount: on list price for bulk; not recorded (only net amount). Cash discount: for prompt payment; recorded (allowed/received).
  • GST: intra-state → CGST + SGST; inter-state → IGST. Output GST (on sales) = liability; input GST (on purchases) = set off via input tax credit.

quiz.q: Which discount is NOT recorded in the books of account?
quiz.explanation: Trade discount is not recorded; only the net amount is.

quiz.q: On an inter-state sale, the GST charged is:
quiz.explanation: Inter-state supplies attract IGST; intra-state attracts CGST + SGST.

questions.q: Subsidiary books are also called books of:
questions.explanation: They are books of original (first) entry.

questions.q: Credit purchases of goods are recorded in the:
questions.explanation: The purchases book records credit purchases of goods.

questions.q: Credit sales of goods are recorded in the:
questions.explanation: The sales book records credit sales of goods.

questions.q: Goods returned to a supplier are recorded in the:
questions.explanation: Returns to suppliers go in the purchases return (return outward) book.

questions.q: Goods returned by a customer are recorded in the:
questions.explanation: Customer returns go in the sales return (return inward) book.

questions.q: The source document for a purchases return is a:
questions.explanation: A debit note supports goods returned to a supplier.

questions.q: Cash purchases of goods are recorded in the:
questions.explanation: Cash purchases go in the cash book, not the purchases book.

questions.q: A credit purchase of machinery is recorded in the:
questions.explanation: Assets bought on credit go in the journal proper.

questions.q: Bills of exchange received are recorded in the:
questions.explanation: Bills received go in the bills receivable book.

questions.q: Opening and closing entries are recorded in the:
questions.explanation: Non-routine entries go in the journal proper.

questions.q: Trade discount is:
options: Not recorded — only the net amount is
questions.explanation: Trade discount is deducted before recording, not entered separately.

questions.q: Cash discount is given to encourage:
questions.explanation: Cash discount rewards prompt payment.

questions.q: On an intra-state sale, GST is charged as:
questions.explanation: Intra-state supplies attract CGST + SGST.

questions.q: GST collected on sales is a:
questions.explanation: Output GST is owed to the government — a liability.

questions.q: List price Rs 10,000, trade discount 20%. Recorded amount:
A firm sells its old delivery van on credit to a garage. This is recorded in the:
options: Journal proper (sale of an asset, not goods)
questions.explanation: The sales book is only for credit sales of goods; selling an asset on credit goes in the journal proper.

questions.q: Goods list price Rs 50,000, trade discount 10%, then 18% GST (intra-state). The invoice total is:
questions.explanation: Net 45,000 after trade discount; GST 18% = 8,100 (CGST 4,050 + SGST 4,050); total 45,000 + 8,100 = 53,100.

questions.q: Why is trade discount never opened as a separate account while cash discount is?
options: Trade discount is deducted before recording; cash discount arises only at payment
questions.explanation: Only the post-trade-discount net figure enters the books, whereas cash discount is an actual gain/expense recorded when payment occurs.

questions.q: Purchases book total for the month is Rs 1,20,000. This is posted to:
questions.explanation: The periodic purchases-book total is debited to the Purchases Account; suppliers are credited individually.

questions.q: A purchase of goods for cash is wrongly entered in the purchases book. The effect is that:
options: Purchases and the supplier are overstated; it should have gone in the cash book
questions.explanation: Only credit purchases of goods belong in the purchases book; a cash purchase belongs in the cash book.

questions.q: Input GST paid on purchases is valuable to a business because it:
options: Can be set off (input tax credit) against output GST payable
Is an expense that lowers profit
questions.explanation: Input tax credit lets the firm reduce its GST liability by the GST already paid on purchases.

questions.q: Which of these correctly pairs the book with its source document?
questions.explanation: When a customer returns goods we issue a credit note, recorded in the sales return book.

questions.q: A wholesaler offers '20% trade discount and 2% cash discount for payment within 10 days'. On a Rs 1,00,000 list order paid in 8 days, the cash paid is:
questions.explanation: Net after 20% trade discount = 80,000; 2% cash discount = 1,600; cash paid = 80,000 − 1,600 = 78,400.

questions.q: The journal proper is best described as:
options: The book for transactions that fit no special book
questions.explanation: It is the residual book for non-routine entries (opening, closing, adjusting, rectifying, asset purchases on credit).

questions.q: On an inter-state sale of Rs 40,000 at 12% GST, the tax charged is:
questions.explanation: Inter-state supplies attract IGST at the full rate: 12% of 40,000 = Rs 4,800 IGST.
